questions.stem: A woman is told she has a blockage in one of her oviducts (fallopian tubes). How would this most likely affect her fertility?

options.text: She would be completely infertile because eggs cannot be released from the ovaries
She would have reduced fertility because eggs from the blocked side cannot travel to the uterus or meet sperm
It would have no effect because eggs can travel through the uterus wall instead
She would be completely infertile because the menstrual cycle would stop

questions.explanation: The oviducts carry eggs from the ovaries to the uterus, and fertilisation normally occurs in the oviduct. If one oviduct is blocked, eggs released from that ovary cannot reach the sperm or the uterus. However, the other ovary and oviduct may still function normally, so fertility is reduced but not eliminated.

questions.stem: During the menstrual cycle, the uterus lining thickens in preparation for pregnancy. If fertilisation does not occur, what happens next and why?

options.text: The lining remains thick until the next egg is released
The lining is broken down and shed as menstruation because progesterone levels drop
The lining is reabsorbed into the bloodstream to save nutrients
The lining thickens further to prepare for the next cycle

questions.explanation: If the egg is not fertilised, the corpus luteum in the ovary degenerates, causing progesterone levels to fall. Without progesterone to maintain it, the thickened uterus lining breaks down and is shed along with blood through the vagina. This is menstruation (a period), and it marks the start of a new cycle.

questions.stem: A scientist observes that a human egg cell is much larger than a sperm cell. Which explanation best accounts for this size difference?

options.text: The egg needs to be large enough for the sperm to find it
The egg contains food reserves (cytoplasm) to nourish the early embryo after fertilisation
The egg is larger because it contains twice as many chromosomes as the sperm
The egg is larger because it must swim through the oviduct to meet the sperm

questions.explanation: The egg cell is much larger than a sperm cell because it contains a large amount of cytoplasm with nutrient reserves. These reserves provide energy and raw materials for the early cell divisions of the embryo before implantation. Both egg and sperm contain the same number of chromosomes (23 each, as haploid cells).

questions.stem: Ovulation typically occurs around day 14 of a 28-day menstrual cycle. A couple trying to conceive would have the best chance of success if intercourse occurs:

options.text: During menstruation (days 1-5) when the uterus lining is being shed
On days 1-3 after the period ends
Around days 12-16, close to when the egg is released
On days 22-28, just before the next period begins

questions.explanation: Ovulation occurs around day 14, and the egg survives for about 12-24 hours after release. Sperm can survive in the female reproductive tract for up to 5 days. Therefore, intercourse in the days just before and around ovulation (days 12-16) gives the best chance of sperm being present when the egg is released.

questions.stem: The cervix produces mucus that changes consistency during the menstrual cycle. Around the time of ovulation, the mucus becomes thinner. What is the biological significance of this change?

options.text: Thin mucus prevents bacteria from entering the uterus
Thin mucus blocks sperm to prevent fertilisation after ovulation
Thin mucus allows sperm to pass through the cervix more easily, increasing the chance of fertilisation
Thin mucus helps the egg travel from the ovary to the uterus

questions.explanation: Around ovulation, oestrogen causes cervical mucus to become thinner and more watery. This allows sperm to swim through the cervix more easily, increasing the likelihood of fertilisation when the egg has just been released. At other times in the cycle, the mucus is thicker and acts as a barrier to sperm.
